{"component_objects":{"details_1":{"type":"grok_share","data":{"profile_user":{"id_str":"0","name":"","verified":false,"is_blue_verified":false},"grok_user":{"id_str":"1720665183188922368","profile_image_url_https":"https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/2057885623374290944/lmj0pawP.jpg","name":"Grok","screen_name":"grok","highlighted_label":{"description":"SpaceX Super Intelligence","badge":{"url":"https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/2108973816865067008/eES3dbLy_bigger.jpg"},"url":{"urlType":"DeepLink","url":"https://twitter.com/SpaceXSI"},"userLabelType":"BusinessLabel","userLabelDisplayType":"Badge"},"verified":false,"is_blue_verified":true,"verified_type":"Business"},"id":"bGVnYWN5_2b134790-72b8-47d6-b182-afb9b775bd6a","conversation_preview":[{"message":"How is this useful?","sender":"USER","grokMode":"NORMAL","mediaUrls":[],"deepsearchHeaders":[]},{"message":"Proving the Riemann Hypothesis (and GRH for Dirichlet \(L\)-functions) is useful primarily because it gives the sharpest possible description of how primes are distributed, and because it turns a large body of existing number-theoretic results from “conditional on RH/GRH” into unconditional theorems.<grok:render card_id="fdb064" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">38</argument></grok:render>
Control over prime numbers
The prime number theorem says the number of primes up to \(x\), written \(\pi(x)\), is asymptotically equal to the logarithmic integral \(\operatorname{li}(x)\). The Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to the strongest known form of the error term:
\[
\pi(x) = \operatorname{li}(x) + O\bigl(\sqrt{x}\,\log x\bigr).
\]
In other words, primes are distributed as evenly as possible; the fluctuations around the main term never grow faster than roughly the square root of \(x\). The version for Dirichlet \(L\)-functions gives the same quality of control for primes in arithmetic progressions.<grok:render card_id="7c202e" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">42</argument></grok:render>
Unlocks many existing results
Hundreds of theorems in analytic number theory have been proved under the assumption of RH or GRH (bounds on gaps between primes, zero-free regions, class numbers, equidistribution results, etc.). Once the hypothesis is established, all of those results become unconditional. The Dirichlet case of GRH is especially useful for statements about primes in arithmetic progressions.<grok:render card_id="e80299" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">40</argument></grok:render>
What it does not do
It does not give a practical algorithm for factoring large integers, and therefore does not break RSA or other public-key cryptosystems that rely on the hardness of factoring. Some primality tests can be made deterministic under GRH, but unconditional polynomial-time primality tests already exist. In short, current encryption is unaffected.<grok:render card_id="9de218" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">35</argument></grok:render>
About this specific formalization
The Lean verification provides extremely high confidence that the mathematical statements are true (multiple independent kernels have accepted the proof and confirmed it matches Mathlib’s definition of RH). However, because there is still no human-readable write-up, the new ideas inside the argument are not yet available for reuse on other problems. Software engineering and research have changed significantly for me.

A big mistake I made early on was trying to automate everything.

Instead of trying to automate everything at once with a bunch of silly and subjective skills, I now spend most of my time helping my coding and research agents write better code and explore novel research ideas.

That's right! I am more involved.

I think this approach works best today, given the current state of coding agents. Not only for coding but for researching as well.

This process has resulted in good patterns codified as loops.

Loops involve automations, but they also include clear, intentional steps you can keep refining to remove jaggedness.

I continually strengthen my loops through verifiers, deterministic steps, context formatting and awareness, memory systems, and evals that steer quality and robustness.

So I agree with other great engineering leaders that our job has fundamentally changed. It's not about using LLMs to help us write code. It's helping the LLM write code better and faster. That's where those loops come into play.

This has significantly reduced error rates and allowed me to expand and scale with coding agents in unbelievable ways. Something I naively expected from my initial, silly, outdated automations.

It feels contradictory at first, since we treat coding agents as solve-it-all intelligence, but it's a system like other traditional systems that requires careful attention to unlock its benefits.

Like my other peers, I believe we are in the early innings. There are more core primitives, interfaces, and experiences to build. For example, we still haven't fully figured out agent swarms.

Coding agents only really started to take off around this time last year. It's unbelievable how much has changed since then.

To be better prepared for what's coming next year, I continue to advocate for gaining deeper knowledge and developing mastery and expertise in your domain. That will continue to matter.

Proving the Riemann Hypothesis (and GRH for Dirichlet \(L\)-functions) is useful primarily because it gives the sharpest possible description of how primes are distributed, and because it turns a large body of existing number-theoretic results from “conditional on RH/GRH” into unconditional theorems.

### Control over prime numbers
The prime number theorem says the number of primes up to \(x\), written \(\pi(x)\), is asymptotically equal to the logarithmic integral \(\operatorname{li}(x)\). The Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to the strongest known form of the error term:

\[
\pi(x) = \operatorname{li}(x) + O\bigl(\sqrt{x}\,\log x\bigr).
\]

In other words, primes are distributed as evenly as possible; the fluctuations around the main term never grow faster than roughly the square root of \(x\). The version for Dirichlet \(L\)-functions gives the same quality of control for primes in arithmetic progressions.

### Unlocks many existing results
Hundreds of theorems in analytic number theory have been proved under the assumption of RH or GRH (bounds on gaps between primes, zero-free regions, class numbers, equidistribution results, etc.). Once the hypothesis is established, all of those results become unconditional. The Dirichlet case of GRH is especially useful for statements about primes in arithmetic progressions.

### What it does *not* do
It does not give a practical algorithm for factoring large integers, and therefore does not break RSA or other public-key cryptosystems that rely on the hardness of factoring. Some primality tests can be made deterministic under GRH, but unconditional polynomial-time primality tests already exist. In short, current encryption is unaffected.

### About this specific formalization
The Lean verification provides extremely high confidence that the mathematical statements are true (multiple independent kernels have accepted the proof and confirmed it matches Mathlib’s definition of RH). However, because there is still no human-readable write-up, the new *ideas* inside the argument are not yet available for reuse on other problems. The main immediate value is settling the truth of RH/GRH; extracting the conceptual content will take further work by mathematicians.

It is also one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems. The prize rules require a refereed publication and a period of community acceptance, so formal verification alone does not immediately award the $1 million.

• 1 Starship upper stage every 2 weeks → ~26 per year

And the scale of what's happening inside is insanely huge

• ~1 MILLION sq ft of manufacturing space
• ~330,000 sq ft of additional office space
• Rows of Starship nose cones numbered as high as Ship 51
• Multiple Starships and boosters being assembled simultaneously
• Most vehicles currently in production are intended to deploy Starlink V3 satellites

There's even a Starship nose cone with windows already cut into it, potentially being developed for NASA's Artemis lunar lander

And SpaceX is preparing to scale production even further

Each of the existing Mega Bays accommodates around 5–6 vehicle assemblies

The massive new ~700,000 sq ft Gigabay under construction at Starbase will have room for up to 24 vehicles simultaneously

That's an enormous expansion in SpaceX's ability to assemble and integrate Starships and Super Heavy boosters

The goal is to reach roughly ONE Starship launch every week beginning in 2027

What's especially impressive is that SpaceX isn't just designing the world's largest rocket anymore. It's also building the manufacturing infrastructure to produce these vehicles at an industrial scale

Starship is no longer just an experimental rocket. It has already moved into payload deployment, and SpaceX is now scaling toward mass production

**No, not in the fully settled sense yet—but there is a major, high-profile claim that it has been proved.**

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge (a mathematician at Anthropic) announced that, working with Claude, he had found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, along with the generalized version for Dirichlet L-functions. He released a short note and a formalization in the Lean proof assistant (roughly 17.4 million lines across ~175,000 files) rather than a conventional paper. He described the full human-readable argument as extremely long (over 250,000 pages in an unpublished version).

Independent checks so far look strong:
- Multiple mathematicians and automated systems (including MIT’s Andrew Sutherland and independent checkers like nanoda) have successfully compiled the Lean code with zero errors.
- It uses only the three standard Lean axioms.
- Experts have described the chance of a serious flaw in the formalization as “approximately zero,” though full human understanding of the argument is still pending because of its size.

The Clay Mathematics Institute (which offers a $1 million prize) has not yet changed the status from unsolved or awarded the prize. Their process requires a published proof, a waiting period, and broad acceptance by the community. A separate, non-AI claim of a proof of a generalized version (by Alessandro Masullo) also appeared around the same time.

In short: There is a machine-checked formal proof that leading reports and mathematicians treat as very likely correct, and it is being treated as a historic development. It is not yet the fully vetted, community-accepted, prize-awarded resolution of the problem. Verification and comprehension work is ongoing.

确实如此，我基于原文稍微解读和引申一下。

很多人说 AI 写不好程序，因为 AI 不能完整理解代码库，但实际上在大的软件项目中，程序员只理解自己负责的一小部分代码是常态。

想象一下，新人去接手一个历史复杂项目，那么他们短时间只可能理解一部分代码，但这并不妨碍他们去维护项目。

那么以前怎么保证不理解完整代码不会改出问题呢？还得要靠自动化测试来兜底。

一个好的项目，需要配合好充分的自动化测试覆盖，这样就算新手去修改代码，也不至于把正常运行的系统搞崩溃，毕竟改出问题了自动化测试是无法通过的。

并且为了防止新人乱改，还会有 Code Review 配合，这本身也是很好的知识传承手段。

现在让 Agent 干活也是如此，让 Agent 在一个会话上下文中理解整个项目是不现实的，它永远只能部分理解项目，但这并不妨碍 Agent 去修改运行程序。

要保证 Agent 干活的质量，同样也要通过验证手段兜底，自动化测试是必须的，但也无法过度依赖，因为有些测试可能本身就是有问题的；

Code Review 现在也很难保证了，毕竟代码量太大了，人根本看不过来，只能是让 AI Review 大部分代码，人只 Review 最重要的部分。

另外一个有效手段就是让 Agent 自己提供证据，比如我最近最常用的手段就是让 Agent 截图，在开发新功能的时候让它提供新功能截图，修改 bug 的时候提供改之前和改之后的截图对比。

让 Agent 截图，最近还挖掘出来一个用法：就是让 Agent 自己去模拟 API 响应数据，动态生成各种不同场景的截图，都不需要服务端配合，虽然我还没搞明白它是怎么去模拟的。

As a software engineer, how well do you have to understand your own codebase?

My guess is that people who work on small codebases with low-turnover teams (say, Redis or games like The Witness) would say “obviously you have to understand it completely, otherwise you can’t do good work”. I’d also guess that people who work on large codebases with high-turnover teams (say, the Google web search backend or GitHub) would say “obviously you can’t understand it completely, you just have to do the best you can in your local area”.

These are two largely different ways of programming with different methods, practices and cultures. However, the first group is over-represented in online discussion about software engineering. I want to defend the second group against the first. In many software engineering environments, there’s nothing wrong with being in a state of partial understanding. In fact, in large systems a partial understanding is the best you can do.

Against “programming as theory building”

The best articulation of the “you have to understand your codebase” side is Peter Naur’s famous paper Programming as Theory Building. I like this paper, but I think it goes too far in that direction. Naur’s core point is that when programmers work on a program, the code is really just a by-product, and the main product they’re working on is their “theory of the program”. That’s made up of their intuitive sense of what’s happening and why, which can only be partially captured by code or documentation. If they lost the code, they could rewrite the program easily. If they lost their understanding (say, if the team experienced 100% turnover), they would struggle to make sense of the code.

• Workers remotely open and close the water gate without physically visiting the site

Workers now have visibility and control over infrastructure that previously required a dangerous mountain trip just to inspect

This becomes especially important during floods and emergencies, when every minute matters and sending workers into dangerous conditions puts lives at risk

只读文字的 AI 审稿人分不清改好的和没改好的论文；把审稿意见写成代码一跑，156 条重大意见里有 77 条推翻了论文结论。编辑读代码时还抓到三篇代码和论文对不上的投稿，其中一篇直接调用了标准答案。

Lauren Tan 写了一份自动化入门指南，核心思路是：先讲清目标，再教 bot 怎么做。

说一点我跟她不一样的地方。

Lauren 自己很强，加上 Grok 模型可能还不够聪明，所以她把更多功夫花在教 Agent 做事上：把自己的最佳实践交给 Grok bot，让它像自己一样思考。

我觉得 AI 比我聪明，用的模型也不局限于 Grok，所以我更强调目标和验收，至于中间的步骤，不太干涉。

我的方法更像一个循环：目标 → 验收 → 改进，一轮一轮转下去。

1. 目标

告诉 AI 我想要什么。这一步谁都一样，必不可少。

2. 验收标准（可选）

告诉 AI 怎么自己检验结果好不好，这样它在把结果交给你之前，会先自己验收一遍。最好再给 Agent 配上验收用的工具，比如截图、网络检索、代码运行环境。

比如我做新闻发布自动化，一条重要的验收标准就是：动笔之前必须先做事实核查，确保内容真实、有出处。

有些任务还可以沉淀出测试集或者自动化测试代码，每次跑完自动验一遍。

3. 先跑起来再调整

目标讲清楚了，就可以先让 Agent 跑一遍看看。就像拿到一把枪，先朝靶子开一枪，打完就知道离靶心差多少、往哪边偏，接下来怎么调心里就有数了。

至于它具体是怎么执行的，不一定要看得很细，现在大部分任务 Agent 都做得挺好。不放心的话，看一看、指导一下也没问题。

调整结果才是最考验专业水准的地方。你自己得知道什么是好的，不然只能 AI 生成什么就接受什么，结果多半好不到哪去。

光看出来不好还不够，还得能准确地描述给 AI，让它知道往哪个方向改。

这样来回几次，结果才会慢慢稳定下来。但不管怎么说，先跑起来最重要，跑起来了才有东西可以优化。

4. 让它自己进化

Agent 有能力自我进化，前提是把经验教训记下来。现在的 Agent Harness 虽然都有记忆功能，但不一定会主动记录自动化任务里遇到的问题。

所以我通常从两个层面，让 Agent 自己提升任务的执行质量。

一个是把最佳实践沉淀成 Skill（包括工具）。比如我给 Agent 一个目标，来回打磨几次，它完成得很好。这时候如果就不管了，下次新开一个会话，记忆就没了；就算去翻历史会话，里面也有太多无关信息。不如趁热让它把这次的最佳实践做成 Skill。

另一个是让它主动记录执行过程中的经验教训，再回头改进 Skill 本身。

比如我做逆向任务，每一轮执行完都让 Agent 往 lessons.md 里记一笔：有教训就写下来，没有就跳过。然后让模型自己评估，要不要去优化 Skill 的说明和脚本。

这样一轮轮下来，Agent 干活就越来越熟练。

这种自我进化也有副作用：Skill 会越来越臃肿，所以要定期重构清理一下，这事交给 Agent 自己做就行。

每次重构完，记得把以前的测试集和自动化测试重新跑一遍，免得删掉不该删的东西。

Lauren 是把人的经验教给 Agent，我是定好目标和验收，让 Agent 自己跑、自己积累经验。模型越聪明，后一种越省心。
